To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the R-gene products of the plant and the Avirulence gene products of the pathogen interact directly to recognize each other and to activate a defense response, and that the Avirulence genes of pathogens may also be able to alter host gene expression in a manner that benefits the pathogen.
R-gene products interact with other host proteins and that these interactions are critical for R-gene function.

(i) plant R-genes encode proteins that recognize cognate Avr-genes and initiate disease resistance responses; and (ii) plant proteins that are required for pathogenicity of the cognate Avr-proteins also function as suppressors of disease-resistance responses.

the molecular basis of disease resistance, and how the proteins encoded by disease-resistance genes function in the plant.

The main takeaway from our work is that

plant disease resistance proteins can be viewed as a type of molecular switch, with the switch being turned on by the Avirulence protein, and the switch turning on other proteins that then mediate disease resistance.

the R-gene products are not simple receptors, but rather complex proteins with many potential functions, some of which might be required for disease resistance and others of which might be important in the normal life of the host.
the R-gene products are likely to have a variety of functions, and that they are unlikely to be the only proteins that interact with the Avirulence products to mediate disease resistance.
